title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
dek: Oil prices haven't spiraled over the past six months thanks to three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. Now all three are being drained, and the real shock is only about to hit diesel and prices.
why: Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil prices haven't risen" into three buffers and their depletion timeline is more useful than reading headlines.
who: Investors and founders watching energy, commodities, and the inflation transmission chain — especially anyone who needs to judge when diesel costs enter their own cost structure.
skip: 09:16 to 10:17, the Venezuela section — low information density, can fast-forward.

points.h: Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
points.body: The war began with Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, immediately cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply. This was the move everyone viewed as the "nuclear option" — no one wanted to see it, because it's too bad for all sides. Once the strait closed, oil prices shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral out of control — it found several buffers to hold prices down. The real question isn't "why did prices rise" but "why didn't they rise more."

points.h: Three buffers, each less durable than the last
points.body: The first is the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve — emergency crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus commercial inventories held by refiners, which were at high levels before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a large "dark fleet" of Iranian and Russian crude floating at sea, which in March the U.S. temporarily allowed other countries to buy. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of global supply. Earlier this year it bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively giving that oil to others. Together, these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

points.h: Ceasefire talks made analysts look foolish en masse
points.body: In June, the U.S. and Iran began peace talks and reached a ceasefire, and market sentiment flipped 180 degrees: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed within weeks, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this round of prices contains a lot of bets on "the war ending soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

points.h: Six months of draining the buffers, and they're nearly dry
points.body: Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves released — and reserves can't be released at will; the government only authorized a specific amount. The U.S. has taken more than 130 million barrels from the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million barrels. That sounds like a lot, but it's approaching the authorized limit. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were hit in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude, it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuels the world needs.

points.h: Venezuela can't put out this fire
points.body: The Trump administration has touted Venezuela as the solution, where reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production capacity is there: to actually raise output, you need to invest money, move rigs, hire people, drill, and ship barrels out — that's roughly years and billions of dollars of investment. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any — you can only hope for "small miracles," like China deciding to boost diesel production, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these will take effect tomorrow.

points.h: Gas stations haven't blown up yet, but diesel has
points.body: U.S. consumers haven't seen price spikes at the gas pump yet; what's really rising is diesel — the fuel that powers the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. The question therefore becomes: will companies cut back on deliveries? When will they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every type of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock transmits from energy markets to the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

points.h: Two paths: absorb it, or pass it on
points.body: Businesses have only two choices. One is to absorb it without raising prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation farmer in Pennsylvania, has raised his beef price only once in five years. Even though the cost of hauling in hay is up 15% to 20%, he eats it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and that holding out will be rewarded. Farmers' exposure to fuel is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, and shipping their own goods out — energy costs can be paid three times over. The second is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil. Some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers raised directly to customers.

points.h: Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
points.body: When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of the woods. Then in August tensions flared again, fuel prices rose again, and recently diesel hit $6 a gallon. Owen thinks this is the moment when some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan commodity analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because they can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and no one — not oil executives, not politicians, not CEOs — can say clearly how long this will last.
